summaries.headline: OpenAI Retiring Custom GPTs for District-Built Tools
summaries.summary: OpenAI is retiring custom GPTs on December 11, 2026, shifting creators toward plugin-based replacements that bundle instructions, reference files and connected apps into a single format. Districts that built custom GPTs for staff or student use will need to manually migrate them, since conversations, custom actions and sharing permissions do not transfer automatically, and Enterprise workspaces face an earlier October 26, 2026 cutoff for creating new GPTs. Technology leaders who rolled out custom GPTs for internal workflows now have roughly two months to inventory what's in use, test migrated plugins for accuracy, and reconfigure access before the originals go dark.

summaries.headline: Google, UN Offer 100,000 Global AI Scholarships
summaries.summary: Google and the UN's International Telecommunication Union are offering 100,000 AI training scholarships across more than 80 countries, giving students, educators, civil servants and job seekers access to the Google AI Professional Certificate with no technology background required. The program, delivered through the ITU's AI Skills Coalition and local governments, lets national and local leaders tailor training to specific needs, such as helping teachers plan lessons faster or helping small business owners grow, and arrives as the ITU estimates 1.2 billion people worldwide still need basic digital skills training. Google and the ITU plan to track completion rates and how learners actually apply new skills in education and employment, a measurement approach that signals growing pressure on large-scale AI literacy initiatives to prove practical impact rather than just reach.

summaries.headline: Nevada Weighs Fixes to Enrollment-Based Funding Formula
summaries.summary: Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo signed emergency regulation releasing $13.4 million in funding to help districts cope with budget shortfalls, including a nearly $52 million gap at Clark County School District tied to declining enrollment and rising employee costs, but lawmakers on both sides say the fix is temporary and point to the 2019 per-pupil formula as the root problem. That formula ties state aid directly to actual enrollment counts, meaning districts lose funding when student populations drop below projections, and legislators are now discussing a "hold harmless" provision to prevent steep cuts while still allowing increases when enrollment grows, alongside possible revenue from ending tax abatements for data centers and CCSD's push to shift the student count used for funding to the spring. With Nevada per-pupil spending still running about $4,000 below the national average, the debate heading into the February legislative session centers less on emergency patches and more on whether the state's funding architecture itself needs a structural overhaul.

summaries.headline: Delaware Moves From Formula Theory to Rollout
summaries.summary: Delaware education officials are now building the implementation infrastructure for a new hybrid school funding formula, following two bills signed this summer that cleared the way to replace an 85-year-old system still reliant on decades-old property assessments in some counties. The Department of Education is consolidating a dozen or more existing funding streams into three categories — base, opportunity, and operational — while four subgroups work through variables on equalization, multilanguage learners, career and technical education, and low-income student funding before bringing recommendations back to the full commission. An earlier test run of the formula showed six of seven sample schools gaining roughly $1.29 million each while a high-needs elementary school stood to lose over $181,000, a result commissioners rejected and that still shadows the technical work now underway to ensure the final model doesn't shortchange the students it was designed to help.

summaries.headline: Credit Union, Toyota Fund Mobile Financial Literacy Classroom
summaries.summary: Truliant Federal Credit Union and Toyota donated $200,000 and a truck to Junior Achievement of the Triad to launch a mobile classroom that will bring financial literacy lessons directly to schools. Inside, students take part in a real-world simulation where they're assigned a career, dependents, and sometimes debt, then navigate budgeting, interest, and savings decisions tied to that scenario, with organizers projecting the unit will reach about 5,000 students annually once it begins visiting classrooms in the 2027-28 school year. The program pairs money-management basics with career exploration tied to local employers, betting that students retain financial concepts better when they're forced to apply them to a simulated life rather than a worksheet.

summaries.headline: College Coaches Add Financial Literacy to Playbook
summaries.summary: Missouri State head coach Cuonzo Martin is incorporating financial literacy instruction into his program as Name, Image and Likeness deals reshape college athletics, with some athletes now receiving substantial paychecks tied to their personal brand. Sophomore Trey Williams, coming off a standout rookie season, said he dismissed thoughts of transferring, citing his relationship with Martin as a key factor in staying. The shift signals how coaches are adapting their roles beyond athletics to address the financial realities now facing student-ath

summaries.headline: Texas Sends Six-Year-Olds to Disciplinary Campuses
summaries.summary: Texas school districts placed nearly 4,000 elementary students into disciplinary alternative education programs (DAEPs) in 2022-23, with state law permitting placements for any child 6 or older and no cap on how long they can last. One McKinney kindergartner was assigned to a DAEP for 30 days over an alleged assault on a teacher, with the placement letter dated the exact day he turned 6 — the minimum age allowed under state law — despite his mother's unsuccessful efforts to get him evaluated for a disability that might have triggered special education protections. Researchers warn that removing young children from class, even briefly, can trigger academic and social setbacks that compound over time, raising questions about whether DAEPs built for serious infractions are being used as a catch-all for behavior schools are unequipped to support.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Member Resigns Amid Internal Conflict
summaries.summary: Denver school board member DJ Torres resigned Thursday, saying “too much of my time and energy have been consumed by internal conflict” rather than student-focused work. His exit follows a public dispute with Board President Xóchitl Gaytán, who had accused Torres and Vice President Monica Hunter of a long list of policy violations — including missed meetings, an unauthorized directive to the superintendent, and refusal to communicate by phone — allegations Torres disputed even as he cited strain on his mental health and family. The resignation leaves District 3 without representation for up to 60 days under state law, underscoring how prolonged governance infighting can sideline the policy work boards are elected to do.

summaries.headline: Denver Board Fast-Tracks Antisemitism Probe Amid Turmoil
summaries.summary: The Denver school board voted to redo a botched investigation into allegations that Vice President Monica Hunter used antisemitic language toward a colleague, giving outside investigators just one week to deliver findings before the board decides whether to censure her. The board initially limited interviews to four people — Hunter, board president Xóchitl Gaytán, board member Amy Klein Molk, and Superintendent Alex Marrero — before expanding the scope at Hunter's request to include other witnesses, even as Gaytán warned that doing so would raise costs and extend the timeline under the board's $1,000-an-hour outside counsel. The episode unfolded alongside the resignation of board member DJ Torres, who cited exhaustion from "internal conflict," leaving the board to fill a vacant seat and treasurer post while managing a dispute that has consumed months of its public meetings.

summaries.headline: St. Mary's County Cuts Chronic Absenteeism By 4.6 Points
summaries.summary: St. Mary's County Public Schools reduced chronic absenteeism to 23.1% by June 2026, down from 27.7%, with officials reporting continued gains into the current school year. The district's tiered intervention system scales from schoolwide prevention—attendance incentives, automated calls, family engagement—up to individualized wraparound support for students missing 20% or more of the school year, including partnerships with health, social services and behavioral health agencies. District leaders framed the drop as meaningful progress while stressing that excused absences still count toward chronic status and that missing just two days a month can total 20 days a year, underscoring how routine, seemingly minor absences compound into significant instructional loss.

summaries.headline: NYC After-School Contract Shakeup Leaves Programs Scrambling
summaries.summary: New York City's Department of Youth and Community Development re-bid after-school contracts for the first time in years, affecting more than 100,000 elementary and middle school students and in some cases replacing providers who had served schools for over a decade. The fallout has been swift: the YMCA of Greater New York is already withdrawing from two Upper West Side middle schools less than a month into the school year after failing to staff programs, while at Yorkville East Middle School — where about 70% of roughly 250 students used after-school programming last year — the principal has resorted to coaching soccer herself and funding staff through a grant set to expire in mid-October. City officials point to 10,000 added seats and updated pay rates of $4,000 to $7,000 per student as justification for the overhaul, but the on-the-ground disruption suggests the transition plan underestimated what it takes to replace staff who were, as one parent put it, "woven into the community."

summaries.headline: OpenAI Academy Adds Dedicated Courses for Educators
summaries.summary: OpenAI has expanded its Academy platform with role-based learning paths, including a dedicated AI for Educators course alongside tracks for developers, organizational leaders and college students. The educator course has teachers work directly with their own class materials to plan lessons, build assessments and adapt communications, while explicitly framing the teacher as responsible for reviewing AI outputs against learning objectives and source material rather than accepting them outright; learners earn OpenAI Academy badges after passing course assessments, and institutions can pair the educator track with OpenAI's broader AI Foundations training. As districts weigh how to structure AI training for staff, OpenAI's move toward role-specific pathways — rather than one-size-fits-all modules — signals where vendor-driven professional development in this space may be heading.

summaries.headline: Handshake, OpenAI Turn AI Practice Into Portfolio Proof
summaries.summary: Handshake has launched AI Skills Studio, a project-based learning initiative with OpenAI as founding partner, aimed at helping students and early-career learners build practical AI skills they can show employers rather than just claim on a resume. The first mission asks participants to use ChatGPT Work to design, build, test and publish a working multiplayer game with no prior coding experience required, then add the finished project to their Handshake profile; a linked competition offers $1,000 prizes to top entries judged on execution and creativity. The effort reflects a broader shift toward treating demonstrated AI-assisted work, not just coursework or credentials, as evidence of career readiness — a framing that higher ed and workforce-focused K-12 programs will likely watch closely as they build their own AI literacy pathways.

summaries.headline: AMD Buys Spatial AI Startup, Hires Fei-Fei Li
summaries.summary: AMD has agreed to acquire World Labs, a spatial intelligence research startup, in an all-stock deal valued at approximately $8.2 billion, with co-founder Dr. Fei-Fei Li joining as Executive Vice President and Chief Scientist once the deal closes by the end of 2026. World Labs develops models focused on understanding 3D environments, robotics and physical AI rather than language alone, and Li's own commentary on the move specifically names learning as one of several domains — alongside drug discovery, creativity and robotics — where she expects increasingly capable AI systems to have impact. For education leaders tracking where frontier AI research dollars and talent are flowing, this signals that major chipmakers are betting on AI's expansion well beyond text-based tools, with unspecified but real implications for how future AI systems might eventually be applied to instructional contexts.

summaries.headline: AI Authorship Scandal Sparks "Era of Suspicion"
summaries.summary: A literary scandal over an award-shortlisted author allegedly using AI to substantially write their book has ignited what French journalist Augustin Trapenard calls an "era of suspicion" toward written work. The IAPP's Isabelle Roccia notes this reaction differs sharply from society's more tolerant stance toward AI use in film, raising questions about whether existing guardrails—legal, technological, or ethical—can actually protect intellectual and emotional integrity when authorship itself is in doubt. The piece leaves open a thornier question for any field built on trust in authentic work: if audiences are duped about origin, does that make the emotional or intellectual response they had any less real.

summaries.headline: Adult Literacy Nonprofit Marks 40 Years, Expands Reach
summaries.summary: Reach Literacy, a Sioux Falls-based nonprofit focused on adult literacy, is marking its 40th anniversary with an expansion of services alongside its annual Brewhaha fundraiser on October 15. The organization is reinstating a prison tutoring program it first launched in 1986 but later discontinued, and is partnering with Siouxland Library locations to offer free literacy classes, with all fundraiser proceeds supporting the work. For district leaders tracking community literacy infrastructure, the move signals a local nonprofit doubling down on adult education access points beyond the K-12 system.

summaries.headline: Andreessen-Backed Academy Offers College Alternative for Grads
summaries.summary: Gagan Biyani, co-founder of Udemy and Maven, has launched the Horowitz Andreessen Academy in San Francisco with $42 million led by Andreessen Horowitz, positioning it as an alternative to traditional college for recent high school graduates. The first cohort enters a tuition-free, one-year Founding Class Fellowship built around self-directed "pursuits," at least three months of full-time work inside partner companies — including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and NVIDIA — and a $5,000 travel stipend for independent study abroad, with a longer-term two-year tuition model planned pending regulatory approval. For K-12 leaders advising seniors on postsecondary options, this signals a growing set of well-funded, industry-backed pathways competing directly with four-year degrees for top talent.

summaries.headline: INSEAD Goes All-In on ChatGPT Edu
summaries.summary: INSEAD has entered a campus-wide partnership with OpenAI, rolling out ChatGPT Edu to all students, faculty and staff rather than confining it to specific courses or departments. The business school's roadmap includes AI-powered case studies, personalized learning, agentic workflows for multi-step tasks, and plans to measure learning outcomes, though OpenAI has not specified how those outcomes will be assessed or on what timeline the roadmap will roll out. With programs spanning France, Singapore, Abu Dhabi and San Francisco, INSEAD's approach to institution-wide AI adoption — paired with its stated intent to measure results — offers a test case other higher-ed institutions will likely watch closely.

summaries.headline: Handshake's AI Tutor Matches Human GRE Results
summaries.summary: Handshake has released StudentBench, a free AI-powered GRE tutoring platform, backed by a study of 2,383 adult participants comparing AI tutoring, expert human tutoring, and a no-tutoring control. Pooled AI tutoring produced learning gains statistically equivalent to human tutoring across combined Quantitative and Verbal sections, with human tutoring ahead by just 0.58 adjusted percentage points, though human tutors still held an edge on Verbal specifically; one model, Gemma 4 31B, matched human-level gains at roughly $0.0052 per percentage point versus $4.81 for the study's human-tutoring reference rate. The release coincides with three senior hires — spanning AI research, enterprise strategy and communications — as Handshake builds out Handshake Labs and its AI business, signaling that graduate-exam prep is becoming a proving ground for claims about AI tutoring at scale.

summaries.headline: Microsoft Backs Kerala EdTech Startup's AI Expansion
summaries.summary: Kerala-based startup Wayvida has secured ₹3.25 crore in Microsoft cloud credits to scale its AI-powered platform, which bundles admissions, fee collection, attendance, communication, and learning management into a single system for educational institutions. Founder Gireesh Neyyar, who has more than 20 years in the education sector, says the backing will strengthen the company's AI capabilities and support plans to expand into international markets alongside its existing LMS, ERP, HRMS, and CRM offerings. The deal underscores a broader shift among schools and institutions away from standalone edtech tools toward integrated digital ecosystems, a trend vendors are increasingly building products around.

synthesis.topic_title: 50-State Tracker: Literacy & Reading — Book-Gifting Scales Up as States Back Billions in Reading Fixes
synthesis.whats_happening: State and local leaders are treating early-childhood book access and evidence-based reading instruction as infrastructure, not add-ons. Ohio and Mississippi are highlighting the growth and reach of Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, while Michigan is deploying nine-figure funding behind Science of Reading mandates after historically low proficiency scores.
synthesis.whats_driving: Michigan's $502 million literacy investment follows M-STEP results showing only 38.9% of third graders proficient or advanced in ELA, the lowest mark in the exam's history, alongside NAEP data showing just 25% of fourth graders at or above proficient. That data crisis is pushing states toward multi-pronged interventions—teacher training, tutoring, coaching—rather than single fixes, while book-gifting programs like Imagination Library (300 million books distributed since 1995) are being framed as a complementary home-literacy layer.
state_themes: Early-childhood book-gifting programs are shifting from charitable extras to recognized literacy infrastructure (Ohio, Mississippi).
Severe proficiency data is driving large, dollar-backed state interventions rather than incremental policy tweaks (Michigan).
Community and nonprofit partnerships—United Ways, student groups, local businesses—are functioning as parallel funding and delivery mechanisms alongside state dollars (Ohio, Michigan, Mississippi).
States are pairing funding with systemic supports—PD, coaching, tutoring, early screening—signaling literacy reform is being treated as a full-system problem (Michigan).
Grassroots, student-led fundraising is emerging as a visible on-the-ground complement to top-down state funding (Mississippi).
synthesis.state_snapshots:
**Ohio**: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has grown from zero enrollment in 2019 to more than 6,100 children enrolled across Wayne and Holmes counties, with costs split 50/50 between a state appropriation and local United Way fundraising at roughly $2.60 per child per month (Lexington Herald Leader).

**Michigan**: State lawmakers budgeted $502 million for literacy initiatives—covering Science of Reading training, literacy coaches, curriculum, and tutoring—after M-STEP scores showed only 38.9% of third graders proficient in ELA, the lowest in the assessment's history (Times Herald opinion).

**Mississippi**: A Copiah-Lincoln Community College student is organizing a campus bake sale to fund Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which has distributed more than 300 million books to children since its 1995 founding (Daily Leader).
district_actions: Audit whether local Imagination Library or equivalent book-gifting enrollment is integrated into birth-registration or kindergarten-intake paperwork, as Ohio does through Vital Statistics.
Map current Science of Reading professional learning against state mandates to identify gaps before mid-year compliance checks.
Inventory local nonprofit and business partners (United Ways, community colleges, civic groups) who could co-fund or staff tutoring and book-access programs.
Review early-reading screening data now to flag students needing intervention before proficiency gaps compound, per the Michigan early-warning approach.
Communicate family-literacy strategies (reading aloud, library visits, vocabulary-building) to parents as a low-cost complement to state-funded classroom reforms.
watch_next: Whether Michigan's $502 million literacy investment shows measurable movement in the next M-STEP or NAEP cycle.

Continued expansion of state-subsidized Imagination Library enrollment models in other states following Ohio's 50/50 cost-share structure [VERIFY: unclear if other states use identical funding split].
Local/community fundraising campaigns (e.g., Mississippi's student-led bake sale) as a bellwether for grassroots literacy engagement heading into fall giving season.

GUEST

# Michigan made literacy a priority. Let’s keep the momentum \| Opinion

Alison Bell

Guest Columnist

Oct. 1, 2026, 4:47 a.m. ET

[Share to Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=112964595441805&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thetimesherald.com%2Fstory%2Fopinion%2Fcolumns%2Fguest%2F2026%2F10%2F01%2Fmichigan-has-a-reading-plan-now-it-needs-results-opinion%2F91772845007%2F)[Share to Twitter](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thetimesherald.com%2Fstory%2Fopinion%2Fcolumns%2Fguest%2F2026%2F10%2F01%2Fmichigan-has-a-reading-plan-now-it-needs-results-opinion%2F91772845007%2F&text=Michigan%20made%20literacy%20a%20priority.%20Let%E2%80%99s%20keep%20the%20momentum%20%7C%20Opinion&via=thetimesherald)[Share by email](mailto:?subject=Michigan%20made%20literacy%20a%20priority.%20Let%E2%80%99s%20keep%20the%20momentum%20%7C%20Opinion%20-%20from%20Times%20Herald&body=Michigan%20made%20literacy%20a%20priority.%20Let%E2%80%99s%20keep%20the%20momentum%20%7C%20Opinion%0A%0AAlison%20Bell%2C%20vice%20president%20of%20Western%20Governors%20University%2C%20argues%20that%20policies%20and%20funding%20alone%20won%27t%20improve%20reading%20scores.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20thetimesherald.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thetimesherald.com%2Fstory%2Fopinion%2Fcolumns%2Fguest%2F2026%2F10%2F01%2Fmichigan-has-a-reading-plan-now-it-needs-results-opinion%2F91772845007%2F)

- Michigan has passed new legislation and budgeted over $500 million for literacy initiatives.
- Recent test scores show Michigan third and fourth graders are performing at historic lows in reading.
- The new approach focuses on the Science of Reading, teacher training, and high-impact tutoring.
- Sustained support from teachers, families, and communities is needed for the reforms to succeed.

Earlier this summer, Michigan took significant steps to change how children learn to read. Newly implemented legislation now requires elementary educators who teach reading to complete professional learning grounded in the Science of Reading, while the state's latest education budget further directs substantial new resources toward literacy curriculum, teacher training, tutoring, literacy coaches and other supports.

Those investments are encouraging. But policies and funding alone won't improve reading scores. What happens next in classrooms, schools and homes across Michigan will determine whether these reforms ultimately make a measurable difference for children.

The need for progress is clear. Only 38.9% of Michigan third graders were proficient or advanced in English language arts on the most recent M-STEP assessment, the lowest third-grade performance in the exam's history. The latest National Assessment of Educational Progress, commonly known as the Nation's Report Card, similarly found that just 25% of Michigan fourth graders performed at or above proficient in reading.

As a mother of three, those numbers are difficult to accept. As an educator, however, I also know they are not set in stone.

Decades of research have given us a clearer and more complete understanding of how children learn to read. The National Reading Panel identified explicit, systematic instruction in areas including phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension as essential components of effective reading instruction. That research helped inform what we now commonly call the Science of Reading.

Thankfully, Michigan is increasingly putting that evidence into practice, strengthening literacy curricula and providing schools with additional literacy coaches. The state is also investing in high-impact tutoring and before- and after-school programs to give students additional support when they need it.

This is meaningful progress, but implementing change across hundreds of school districts and thousands of classrooms takes time, consistency and sustained support.

First, we need to ensure teachers have the tools to turn professional learning into everyday classroom practice. Training should not be treated as yet another box to check — teachers are busy enough as is. Rather, educators need purposeful opportunities to deepen their knowledge, collaborate with colleagues and receive ongoing coaching as they put evidence-based strategies to work.

We also need to identify struggling readers early and provide targeted help before they fall further behind. A child who has difficulty reading in the early grades can encounter challenges across nearly every subject later on. Strong screening, evidence-based intervention and individualized support can help schools respond before those difficulties compound.

And the work cannot end when students leave the classroom — families have a role to play as well. Fortunately, I know firsthand that moms and dads don't need to become literacy experts to reinforce good reading habits at home. Small but meaningful changes like reading together, asking children questions about a story, introducing new vocabulary and making trips to the local library can all complement the work happening at school.

Communities can also reinforce that support. Businesses, colleges and community organizations can partner with schools on tutoring and mentoring programs. College students, retirees and other volunteers can donate their time to give young readers additional opportunities to practice. Sustained state funding can also ensure libraries continue to serve as accessible places where families find books, programs and literacy resources.

Michigan has recognized that improving literacy requires going beyond simply hoping reading scores eventually rebound. The state has begun aligning policy, funding and instruction around what research tells us works. In its latest education budget, Michigan committed $502 million toward literacy initiatives, including investments in teacher training, literacy coaches, evidence-based curricula, tutoring and expanded before- and after-school programming.

That should mark the beginning of our work, not the end. The real measure of Michigan's literacy reforms will be whether more of the state’s children are able to become confident, capable readers. What we need now is the sustained commitment to make sure these efforts reach every classroom and every child who needs them.

The work ahead is substantial, but so is the opportunity: to make strong reading skills a foundation Michigan’s children can build on for a lifetime.

_Alison Bell is regional vice president of Western Governors University._

## Co-Lin student is ‘Baking for a Cause’: Literacy

Published 9:00 am Thursday, October 1, 2026

**By [Brett Campbell](https://dailyleader.com/author/brett-campbell/)**

![](https://dailyleader.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/18/2026/09/web-Anna-McKenzie.jpg?w=1024)

PHOTO SUBMITTED
Anna McKenzie

|     |
| --- |
| **Getting your [Trinity Audio](https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...** |

As a member of Phi Theta Kappa at Copiah-Lincoln Community College, Anna McKenzie has combined several of her passions into a one-day project — “Baking for a Cause.”

At Co-Lin, McKenzie is Vice President of Scholarship for PTK, as well as president of the Student Government Association. As a PTK officer, McKenzie has the opportunity to work on a “Passion Project.”

The sophomore chose to combine several of her passions and interests — baking, event planning, photography, business, and literacy — “into something meaningful that could make a difference beyond just our campus,” she said.

“Baking for a Cause” will be a bake sale on Thursday, Oct. 8, at the Co-Lin Homecoming Tailgate prior to the game against East Central Community College. All proceeds from the sale will go to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, which provides free, high-quality books to children from birth to age 5. Since its founding in 1995, the program has provided more than 300 million books to children worldwide.

“This project is especially meaningful to me because I had the opportunity to work at Dollywood’s Splash Country in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, this summer,” McKenzie said. “During my time there, I experienced so much kindness, love, and hospitality, and I saw firsthand how deeply Dolly Parton’s values of giving and helping others were woven into the culture surrounding her. I believe a book is so much more than just a book. It can be a doorway to imagination, a source of comfort, a place to learn, and the beginning of a lifelong love of reading.”

“Every child deserves the opportunity to have books at home and to experience the joy of reading. To me, this project is about so much more than just selling baked goods,” she said. “It’s about planting a small seed of kindness and watching it grow into something that can reach children far beyond our own community.”

## Subscribe to our free email newsletter

Get the latest news sent to your inbox

McKenzie’s goal is for this project to impact more than just the Co-Lin campus community.

“We are searching for individuals, families, local businesses and bakeries, and anyone in the community who would be willing to donate baked goods for the bake sale. Monetary donations are also greatly appreciated,” the Smithdale native said. “Word of mouth is huge. We never know how much a small act of kindness might affect someone else.”

After Co-Lin, the hospitality and tourism major plans for a future that allows her to travel, meet new people, and create experiences for others.

“I hope our community will come together to raise money for something bigger than any one of us and help give children the opportunity to discover the joy, imagination, and possibilities that come from having a book of their own,” McKenzie said. “If you know anyone who loves to bake, please spread the word!”

For more information on “Baking for a Cause” or to discuss donating baked items or funds, contact McKenzie at 601-757-7099 or annamckenziet@icloud.com.

local_articles.title: Dolly Parton Day highlights literacy program growth
local_articles.summary: Dolly Parton Day highlights literacy program growth  Lexington Herald Leader
local_articles.full_content:
![Commissioner Dave McMillen, Commissioner Jonathan Hofstetter, United Way Wayne and Holmes Counties Board member Clay Matthew, United Way Wayne and Holmes Counties Community Relations Manager Kayley Cox, Board President Bonnie Hall, and Commissioner Matt Martin pose together with samples of books that are distributed to children up to five years old in Wayne and Holmes counties.](https://www.mcclatchy-wires.com/public/incoming/kwfs0u/picture317436397/alternates/LANDSCAPE_1200/e1b15b53-ecb7-4109-b701-8fe359363c88)



Commissioner Dave McMillen, Commissioner Jonathan Hofstetter, United Way Wayne and Holmes Counties Board member Clay Matthew, United Way Wayne and Holmes Counties Community Relations Manager Kayley Cox, Board President Bonnie Hall, and Commissioner Matt Martin pose together with samples of books that are distributed to children up to five years old in Wayne and Holmes counties.




Provided by Dan Starcher
USA TODAY Network, Reuters

WAYNE COUNTY-Gov. Mike DeWine and Lt. Gov. Jim Tressel proclaimed Friday, Sept. 25, as Dolly Parton Day in Ohio, recognizing Parton's life, legacy, and work to promote childhood literacy through Dolly Parton's Imagination Library.

The date, 9/25, also coincides with the first Give Like Dolly Day and references Parton's hit song "9 to 5."

The recognition comes as Dolly Parton's Imagination Library continues to expand in Wayne and Holmes counties, where more than 6,100 children are currently enrolled, according to United Way Wayne and Holmes Counties (UWWH) Community Relations Manager Kayley Cox. The local program has grown from essentially no enrollment when the statewide effort began in 2019 to serving thousands of children across the two counties.

"It literally went from zero in seven years to over 6,100 kids between the two counties," Cox said. "The program gives children access to age-appropriate books every month, and it gives families that reminder to sit down, read, and have that time together."

Research compiled by the Dollywood Foundation has found that participation in Imagination Library programs is associated with changes in home literacy practices. Studies reviewed by the foundation found parents reported reading aloud more frequently, children owned more books, and participating children showed greater interest in reading.

Some studies also found that children participating demonstrated more advanced early literacy skills than classmates who did not participate, although the foundation notes much of the research has been conducted at the local community level.

"It really brings us back to the basics," Cox continued. "The child sees the book, it has their name on it, and they want to open their mail. It reminds families that it's time to sit down and read and have that family togetherness and bonding through a book."

Funding for Dolly Parton's Imagination Library is shared among the program's state and local partners, including the Orrville Area United Way who is the local program partner for Orrville, Dalton and Marshallville.

Dolly Parton's Imagination Library of Ohio oversees a state appropriation that covers 50% of the cost of books and postage, while local program partners, including UWWH, raise the remaining 50%. The cost is approximately $2.60 per child per month. The Dollywood Foundation covers overhead and administrative expenses and coordinates book selection, production, fulfillment, and shipping. United Way also covers its local administrative expenses associated with enrolling children, maintaining the participant database, and building community partnerships to encourage enrollment.

"We have a 50% cost share through the state of Ohio," Cox said. "It's still $30 per child per year because we never know what's going to happen fundraising-wise. That's $2.60 times 12 months times 6,100 kids-it adds up."

Cox said United Way also manages the local enrollment database, including updating addresses and removing duplicate or inactive records, to help ensure books reach the children enrolled in the program. "We make sure it's as up to date as possible," she said. "If a child doesn't change their address, the book becomes undeliverable. We make sure to take them out of the system or update their address."

Ohio families can also begin participating in the Imagination Library as soon as a child is born. Parents can choose to enroll their newborn through the state's Vital Statistics paperwork by checking the Imagination Library enrollment option. The Ohio Department of Health then helps place those children into the Imagination Library system. Children not enrolled at birth can be signed up later, any time before their fifth birthday, and every eligible child in a family can participate.

Parents and caregivers can enroll an eligible child through Dolly Parton's Imagination Library of Ohio. Information about the Wayne and Holmes County program and local donations is available through UWWH at www.uwwh.org.
